epithet: Turjuman al-Quran (Interpreter of the Quran); Hibr al-Ummah (Scholar of the Ummah); Ra'is al-Mufassirin (Chief of the Exegetes)
role: Foremost Quranic exegete among the Sahaba
Governor of Basrah under Ali ibn Abi Talib
summary: Abdullah ibn Abbas (RA) was the cousin of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, born into the Banu Hashim clan, and the foremost scholar of Quranic exegesis (tafsir) among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ. Known as Turjuman al-Quran (Interpreter of the Quran) and Hibr al-Ummah (Scholar of the Ummah), his explanations of Quranic verses form the foundational layer of all major classical tafsir works, and his intellectual legacy shaped Islamic scholarship for over a millennium.
biography:
Abdullah ibn Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib al-Hashimi al-Qurashi was born around 619 CE in Makkah, approximately three years before the Hijrah. His father al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib was the Prophet's paternal uncle and one of the most prominent men of Quraysh. His mother Umm al-Fadl Lubabah bint al-Harith al-Hilaliyyah is described in classical sources as among the earliest women to accept Islam after Khadijah bint Khuwaylid (RA). Abdullah was born into a household already on the verge of Islam.

As a young child, he was brought by his mother to the Prophet ﷺ, who blessed him and reportedly said: 'O Allah, give him understanding in religion and teach him the interpretation (ta'wil).' In another narration in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet ﷺ placed his hand on Ibn Abbas's chest and said: 'O Allah, fill him with wisdom.' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab al-Ilm). These prophetic supplications are cited by all classical scholars as the divine source of his exceptional scholarly gifts.

Ibn Abbas was too young to be considered among the Sahaba who participated in the great early battles, but he grew up in the Prophet's household during the Madinan period and had significant direct exposure to the Prophet ﷺ. After the Prophet's death, he dedicated himself to the pursuit of knowledge with a rigor and discipline that is among the most celebrated examples of scholarly commitment in Islamic history.

He is reported to have gone from house to house among the Sahaba, asking each one to teach him whatever hadith they knew from the Prophet ﷺ. When a companion was asleep at midday, Ibn Abbas would wait at the door, sitting on the ground and allowing the dust and heat of Madinah to accumulate on him, rather than wake the companion. When the companion woke and found him there, he would apologize that Ibn Abbas had not woken him, to which Ibn Abbas replied: 'Seeking knowledge is an obligation I must not be casual about.' (Various Seerah and hadith source collections; al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, Ibn Sa'd, Vol. 2)

His scholarly relationship with Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) is particularly noteworthy. Despite the difference in age between them, Umar included Ibn Abbas in his consultative council — the circle of senior companions whose opinions he sought on difficult questions of governance and law. When some senior Sahaba objected that Ibn Abbas was too young for this circle, Umar reportedly convened a session in which he posed a difficult question about the Quranic verse on the nasr (victory) surah, and the senior companions gave various answers. Ibn Abbas gave the answer that matched Umar's own understanding — that the surah was an announcement to the Prophet ﷺ of the approaching end of his life. Umar told the assembled companions: 'This is what I meant.' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab al-Tafsir — Surah al-Nasr; this account is one of the most famous examples of Ibn Abbas's early scholarly recognition)

As an exegete, Ibn Abbas's methodology was distinguished by: reliance on the Quran explaining itself (tafsir al-Quran bi-l-Quran), extensive use of authentic hadith, recourse to the pre-Islamic Arabic poetry to determine linguistic meanings of Quranic vocabulary, and careful attention to the asbab al-nuzul (occasions of revelation) — the specific circumstances in which each verse was revealed. His explanations of Quranic verses were transmitted by his students and form the primary layer of tafsir in the works of al-Tabari (Tafsir al-Tabari), Ibn Kathir (Tafsir Ibn Kathir), and virtually all subsequent classical tafsir literature. When classical exegetes write 'Ibn Abbas said about this verse...', they are drawing on a tradition of transmission that goes back through chains of narrators to his direct statements.

Among his most famous students in tafsir were: Sa'id ibn Jubayr (the greatest of his students, martyred by al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf), Mujahid ibn Jabr (whose tafsir notes from Ibn Abbas's dictation are the oldest surviving major tafsir document), Ikrimah (the freed slave of Ibn Abbas), Ata ibn Abi Rabah, and Tawus ibn Kaysan. Together, these students formed the 'Makkan school' of tafsir, named for the city where Ibn Abbas taught, which is considered one of the three foundational schools of early tafsir alongside the Madinan and Iraqi schools.

In fiqh, Ibn Abbas was known for independent reasoning (ijtihad) that sometimes differed from the positions of other major Sahaba. He was among the more permissive of the Sahaba in certain questions — a quality that led both to broad acceptance of his rulings among later jurists and occasional scholarly disagreement with specific positions. The Shafi'i and Hanbali schools in particular drew heavily on his fiqh opinions, and many of the issues on which he is cited in classical fiqh literature involve questions of inheritance, marriage, and ritual purification.

Politically, Ibn Abbas supported Ali ibn Abi Talib (RA) during the fitna period and served as governor of Basrah under him. He participated in the negotiations after the Battle of Siffin and was among those who accepted the arbitration decision — unlike the Khawarij who split from Ali over this issue. After the death of Ali (40 AH), he withdrew from political life, eventually settling in Ta'if, where he died.

He lost his eyesight in his later years — a trial he bore with patience. He died in Ta'if in 68 AH (687 CE) at approximately 68 years of age. His funeral prayer was reportedly led by Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah (son of Ali ibn Abi Talib). His legacy is not limited to any sect or school: both Sunni and Shia scholars venerate him as a primary source of religious knowledge, and his tafsir continues to be quoted in Islamic scholarship to this day.

The Prophet ﷺ had prayed for him: 'O Allah, give him understanding (fiqh) in religion.' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab al-Wudu'). This supplication was answered in full — in the estimation of every major classical scholar, no figure produced more foundational knowledge of the Quran's meaning than Abdullah ibn Abbas (RA).

key_events.event: Born in Makkah to al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib and Umm al-Fadl
Came to Madinah as a child; lived near the Prophet ﷺ in his Hashimi household
Present at the death of the Prophet ﷺ; began systematic collection of knowledge from the Sahaba
Included by Umar ibn al-Khattab in his scholarly consultative council despite his young age
Supported Ali ibn Abi Talib as legitimate Caliph during the fitna
Appointed governor of Basrah by Ali ibn Abi Talib
Withdrew to Makkah after Ali's death; devoted remaining decades to teaching

notable_traits: Prophetically gifted with understanding of the Quran — direct result of the Prophet's du'a
Extraordinary scholarly humility — would wait at the door of companions rather than disturb their rest
Intellectual independence — gave opinions based on evidence even when they differed from senior companions
Encyclopedic knowledge: Quran, hadith, Arabic linguistics, pre-Islamic poetry, and history
Founded the 'Makkan school' of tafsir that influenced all subsequent Quranic scholarship

key_relationships.father: al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib (uncle of the Prophet ﷺ)
key_relationships.mother: Umm al-Fadl Lubabah bint al-Harith al-Hilaliyyah (among earliest female Muslims)
key_relationships.prophetic_connection: Cousin of the Prophet ﷺ; from Ahl al-Bayt (Banu Hashim)

narrated_hadith_count: approximately 1,660 hadith in the major collections
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari — Kitab al-Ilm; Kitab al-Tafsir (extensive, throughout)
Sahih Muslim — Kitab al-Tafsir and throughout
al-Tabari, Tafsir al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) — Ibn Abbas is the most-cited source
Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Quran al-Adhim — extensive reliance on Ibn Abbas
Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, al-Isabah fi Tamyiz al-Sahaba
